Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:21: And so, along these lines, King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 8:4), "when I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon," and so on - and the explanation is that King David, peace be upon him, was not looking at the physical heavens visible to the eyes, but at their inner spirituality, which is the work of His blessed fingers, the ten supernal sefirot - and this is also his saying, "the moon and stars that You have established" - it was at their establishment that he gazed, for through the establishment of the lower one the deed of the supernal one is discerned and recognized.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:22: And concerning the aspect of the repair of "humble eyes," one must conduct oneself with the qualities of Rabbi, peace be upon him, one of the ten qualities he had being that he would not look beyond four cubits, and his face would turn toward the ground and not to the sides, so as not to see any transgression.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:23: And further it appears to me that in looking at the ground he should think that he is dust and to dust he shall return, and not think of the passing and perishing affairs of this world - and a person must conduct himself with this repair while he is in his house, so that he be trained for when he walks in the marketplace or a place where nakedness is found, that he not gaze at nakedness. And so, if he is trained within his house not to look beyond four cubits, so as not to remove fear from himself, thinking as though he stands before the King, he shall gain from this that it will be easy for him to fulfill this measure when he stands in the synagogue occupied with prayer, when it is not fitting to distract his mind to look beyond four cubits, as we shall elaborate concerning prayer, with God's help. The general rule is that every matter of piety a person must first fulfill within his house, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 101:2), "I will walk within my house with a perfect heart" - and afterward it will be easy for him to fulfill it when he is outside his house. And concerning this King Solomon, peace be upon him, commanded and said (Proverbs 4:25), "let your eyes look straight ahead, and your eyelids look straight before you" - and the plain sense of the verse is that when he considers that the Shechinah is opposite him, it is a disgrace for a servant to gaze at the face of his master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:24: And along these lines, the reason for not looking beyond four cubits is that one must equate his measure to his Master's measure - for just as concerning His blessed eyes it is written (Deuteronomy 11:12), "the eyes of the LORD your God are always upon it," and its measure is four cubits, corresponding to the number of the four letters of Adonai, so must one conduct himself. When a person conducts himself with this measure, he unifies the Name Yud-Alef-Heh-Dalet-Vav-Nun-Kuf-Yud [YHVH+Adonai combined], for in the eye is the Name YHVH, as explained above, and when he looks at the ground, which is Adonai (cf. Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, page 84a), he is found unifying - but if he looks outward at what is unnecessary, he separates YHVH from Adonai, because he is haughty of eyes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:25: And the reason, more precisely, is as is known: that any seed cast within the female is not called seed in vain, and sight, which is a supernal light emerging from the "house of the eye," which is the supernal Yud, is like the physical seed emerging from the sign of the covenant, the lower Yud (Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Pinchas, page 256a) - and just as we were commanded not to emit the physical seed in vain, so the matter of sight must not be emitted in vain, meaning not to look at what is unnecessary for him, but that his eyes be [directed] toward the ground, and then it is not in vain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:26: And what we say, that he should not look beyond four cubits, the intent is that for most of his walking he should not look with a full gaze, for then he would be haughty of eyes, and it is written (Psalms 101:5), "haughty of eyes," and so on, "him I cannot endure." But if, incidentally, he raises his eyes into the distance, there is no blemish to the eyes in this - for it is possible that he sees a lost object and returns it, and it is found that through this sight he performs a commandment; and likewise if he sees his teacher in the distance, within eyeshot, he must rise before him, and this too is a commandment, because of "before the aged you shall rise" (Leviticus 19:32) - and so, along these lines, King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 121:1), "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where shall my help come," and so on - and in saying "I lift up," it appears that his manner of walking was with lowered eyes, since he needed to lift up his eyes - and so (Genesis 22:4), "and Abraham lifted up his eyes," and so (ibid. 37:25), "and they lifted up their eyes," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:27: And through this we shall understand (Job 31:1), "I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I look upon a maiden," and so on - and the explanation is that just as there is a covenant of the tongue and a covenant of the flesh, so there is a covenant of the eyes - and the reason is that "covenant" is the secret of the letter Yud, as explained, and just as one must be careful with the lower covenant not to emit seed in vain, so with the covenant of the eyes - and whoever guards the supernal Yud, which is in the pupil, certainly guards the lower Yud, which is in the covenant, as they said, of blessed memory (Ketubot 46a), "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10) - that one should not have lustful thoughts by day and come to impurity at night - and lustful thought comes only through sight, for what he has not seen, how would he have lustful thoughts about it? And this is also because the seed comes from the light of a person's eyes, and whoever guards his sight guards his seed, and whoever blemishes his sight blemishes the seed emerging from the brain and in the lower Yud, as shall be further explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:28: And it is possible to say that the allusion of these two yuds is the yuds in the Alef, and the Vav in the middle of the two yuds is the tongue, which is also called a covenant - and whoever guards these three covenants is bound to YHVH and to His blessed unity, which is the alluded-to Alef, indicating "one" [echad]. And you already know that two yuds and a vav total twenty-six, the numerical value of YHVH - and since he is bound to this unity, no external force, which is "another," has a share in him. And if, Heaven forfend, he blemishes one of these three, it is as though he blemishes the Alef, for the blemish is found in all three, since spirituality is not divided, but is entirely a complete unity - along the lines of what they said in the Tikkunim, "whoever has a blemish shall not approach" (Leviticus 21:18). And therefore happy is the one careful to fulfill these matters, for they are founded on the foundation of the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, and truth shall guide his path.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:29: Further, know that according to what they said in the Tikkunim (page 145b), that the nose is Vav, and according to what was explained above, that the pupil is Yud - so the nose, Vav, is found between two yuds, behold Alef; and when a person has humble eyes, the two yuds unite in the Vav, and he is found unifying YHVH; but if not, Heaven forfend, the yuds are found withdrawn, for there is no uniting Vav between them - and when he is angry or looks in anger, there is judgment in the eyes, and therefore they said (Berachot 58a), "he set his eyes upon him and judgment ruled, and he became a heap of bones."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:30: And the verse "I made a covenant with my eyes" - since it has come to hand, let us say something about it. Since it is relevant to our topic, it is possible to explain it by the plain meaning - what we have introduced, that a person must set a boundary for sight, not to look beyond four cubits - and this is "I made a covenant with my eyes," meaning a statute and boundary - and this is what it says, "how then could I look upon a maiden" - meaning, I gain from this that the occasion to look would not arise even at a maiden, since, having the boundary mentioned, it is impossible for me to come to look. And this is [the meaning of] "how" [u-mah], for it should have said "and I will not look" - rather it is as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:31: Further, it is possible to say that just as the covenant has milah [circumcision] and periah [uncovering], so with the eyes there is a pattern of what is forbidden, which we shall write, with God's help, and this is "milah," which is the foreskin cast outward. However, there are worldly matters that one is permitted to look at, provided he blesses over them - such as one who goes out in the days of Nisan and sees trees blossoming, who blesses "Blessed is He who has made this so in His world and created in it good creatures," and so on (Berachot 43b) - and behold, this benefits himself in seeing the physical thing, and through the blessing he makes over it, he generalizes the physical and makes it spiritual - and similarly all the things mentioned in the Talmud, chapter "HaRo'eh," over which one blesses, such as one who sees the great sea (Berachot, chapter 9, mishnah 2) - this is the aspect of "periah," which is the foreskin included inward in holiness - it follows that in the pattern of the covenant, "I made a covenant with my eyes" means that there be in them both milah and periah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:32: Among the things one must be careful of, some are said in the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 20b), in these words: "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10) - that a person should not gaze at a beautiful woman, even if unmarried; nor at a married woman, even if ugly; nor at colored garments of a woman; nor at a male donkey, a female donkey, a boar, or a sow, nor at birds when they are mating with each other - this is the wording of the Baraita. And it says further in the Talmud there, "nor at colored garments of a woman" - Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel, even spread on a wall. Rav Papa said, and [this applies] when he recognizes their owner. Rava said, this is also precisely indicated, since it teaches "the colored garments of a woman" and not "colorful garments" - infer from this - to this point, their wording. And from this Baraita you learn that since they forbade a woman's garments spread on a wall when one recognizes the woman, all the more so it would be forbidden to look at a bed on which a man and his wife sleep, if he recognizes them - for this arouses the desire of the inclination even more.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:33: Further, we say in Tractate Shabbat (64a), concerning the women of Midian, where it is written (Numbers 31:50), "and we have brought an offering for the LORD, what every man has found, of jewels of gold, armlets," and so on - in these words: it was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael, why did the Israelites of that generation need atonement? Because they feasted their eyes on the nakedness [of the women]. Rav Sheshet said, why did Scripture list the outer ornaments together with the inner ornaments? To tell you that whoever gazes at a woman's little finger is as though he gazed at her private place - to this point. And Rashi explains: "outer ornaments" - a ring; "inner" - a "kumaz" [an ornament worn near the private area]. Whoever gazes at the little finger, which is the place of the ring, is as though he gazed at the place of the kumaz - it is for having gazed that this atonement came - to this point. "Kumaz," we say in the Talmud, is a mold shaped like the womb.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:34: Further, we say in Bava Batra (57b) on the verse (Isaiah 33:15), "and shuts his eyes from looking upon evil" - in these words: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said, this refers to one who does not gaze at women when they are standing at the laundry. How so? If there is another road [he could take], he is wicked [for not taking it]; and if there is no other road, he is forced [and blameless]. Actually, it means there is no other road, and even so he must force himself [to avert his eyes] - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:35: Further, we say in Nedarim (20a): Rabbi Acha bar Yoshiya says, whoever gazes upon women will eventually come to sin, and whoever looks at the heel [akevah] of a woman will have unworthy children. Rav Yosef said, and [this is true even] with his own wife when a niddah. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, the "heel" it teaches of is the place of filth [i.e., the genitals], which is directly opposite the heel - to this point. And right next to this they said there, it was taught: "and so that His fear be upon your faces" (Exodus 20:17/20) - this is shame - "so that you not sin" - this teaches that shame brings one to fear of sin, as we copied in the Gate of Fear, end of chapter 3. And the juxtaposition of this Baraita to the matter of gazing, and so on, is to teach that one must feel shame before his Maker who looks upon him, and through this he will not come to gaze at nakedness or at the covered places of his wife, which are nakedness, as we say (Berachot 24a), "a woman's leg is nakedness," and so on - for from gazing one comes to lustful thought, and comes to impurity, and is found transgressing what is written in the Torah, "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing," as copied above. It follows that shame brings one to fear of sin, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:36: Further, they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Kohelet, remez 976), on the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:26), "one who is good before God shall escape her" - this is one who sees a woman on a bed and flees; "and the sinner shall be caught by her" - this is one who is caught with her - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:37: Further, they said in Tractate Megillah (28a) that it is forbidden to look at the face of a wicked person, in these words, on the verse (2 Kings 3:14), "were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat... I would not look at you, nor see you" - Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said, it is forbidden to gaze at the image of a wicked person, as it is said, "I would not look at you, nor see you." Rabbi Elazar says, [Isaac's] eyes grew dim, as it is said (Genesis 27:1), "and it came to pass, when Isaac was old, that his eyes grew dim," because he had gazed at Esau, and it is written (Proverbs 18:5), "it is not good to regard the face of the wicked" - to this point, their wording. And in Sefer Chasidim (siman 926), one who gazes at his wife when a niddah, and likewise one who gazes at the face of one who is angry, forgets his learning - and these are words of wisdom that need no reinforcing proofs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:38: And in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim, page 83b), further things are said that it is forbidden to gaze at, in these words: we have learned, it is forbidden for a person to gaze at the beauty of a woman, lest he come to an evil lustful thought and be drawn to another matter. And so Rabbi Shimon would do: when he would walk in a town and the colleagues would walk behind him, and he saw beautiful women, he would lower his eyes and say to the colleagues, "do not turn" (Leviticus 19:4) - for whoever gazes at the beauty of a woman by day comes to lustful thought at night, and if that evil lustful thought arises upon him, he transgresses because of "and molten gods you shall not make for yourselves" (ibid.). Further, if he has relations with his wife at the time this evil lustful thought arose in him, the children born from this are called "molten gods." "Do not turn to idols" and "molten gods you shall not make for yourselves." Rabbi Abba said, it is forbidden for a person to gaze at the idols of the nations, and not to derive benefit from them, and not to be healed by them, and all the more so not to gaze at them, for it is forbidden for a person to gaze at a place he does not need - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:39: And from here you shall see the severity of the prohibition of gazing, from what he said at the end of his words, "and all the more so not to gaze at them" - that there is a greater prohibition in gazing than in being healed by them, and he gave the reason for the matter: it is forbidden for a person to gaze at a place he does not need. And the reason is because he turns his mind from holiness toward something vain and empty, and this is along the lines of what they expounded (Shabbat 149a-b), "do not turn to idols" - do not turn to your own opinion - for anything a person does not need to gaze at, and he gazes at it, is external, since the external is what a person does not need, being the refuse of holiness. And so it says in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei, page 263a) that the inclination entices a person to gaze at something unnecessary and to satiate his eyes with the affairs of this world, in order to break his eyes in the grave for every single sight - and every external thing imprinted in thought through his gazing is a blemish in the soul clothed there, as explained above - and it will not seem far when you see how many supernal secrets are in the eye, as we have copied the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:40: And it is found, as a general rule, that whoever gazes at something unnecessary transgresses a positive and a negative commandment - being "turn from evil and do good," for in turning his mind from holiness he transgresses the positive, and in acquiring for his soul the image of that evil, behold, the negative.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:41: And besides this, it is forbidden to gaze at anything that would bring a person to joy, as it says in the Zohar (Parashat Tazria, page 45b), in these words: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yosi were walking on the road; when they came to a certain field, they saw a "petira de-kitfa" [balsam tree] on the right side of the road. Rabbi Yosi said, a wrapping of smoke is upon the eyes; we should not see joy from the day the Temple was destroyed - to this point. And the meaning of "wrapping of smoke" is a covering and binding, or smoke, for the eyes - and the intent is a concealing of the eyes so as not to see joy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:42: Further, it says there (Parashat Kedoshim, page 84a): come and see, it is forbidden for a person to gaze at a place that the Holy One, blessed be He, despises and from which His soul is distant - and if concerning what the Holy One, blessed be He, loves it is forbidden to gaze, how much more so concerning what He distances. And come and see, it is forbidden for a person to gaze at a rainbow, because it is a vision of the supernal image; it is forbidden for a person to gaze at his own sign of the covenant, because it alludes to the righteous one of the world. It is forbidden for a person to gaze at the fingers of the priests when they spread their hands, because there the glory of the supernal King rests. And if in a holy supernal place it is forbidden to gaze, in an impure, distant place, how much more so - and therefore, "do not turn to idols" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:43: Further, there (Parashat Beshalach, page 66b), in these words: it is forbidden to gaze at the rainbow. Which rainbow? Rabbi Abba said, the rainbow simply. What is "the rainbow simply"? He said to him, the supernal rainbow and the lower rainbow. The supernal rainbow, in its colors - for whoever gazes at its colors is as though he gazed at the supernal place, and it is forbidden to gaze at it, so that he not disgrace the Shechinah. The lower rainbow, what is it? That sign of the covenant marked on a person - for whoever gazes at it disgraces above. Rabbi Yitzchak said, if so, is it not written (Genesis 24:2), "put now your hand under my thigh," where he would swear by this sign? He said to him, leave the Patriarchs of the world aside, for they are not like the rest of the world; and further, it is written "put now your hand under my thigh," not "look under my thigh" - therefore it is forbidden to gaze at the rainbow simply, as we have learned - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:44: And it says in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah 9:11), that this is why he was called "Rabbeinu HaKadosh" [our holy Rabbi], because he never in his life looked at his own circumcision. Antoninus said to Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi], when you were circumcised, did you look at your circumcision? He said to him, I never looked at my own; would I look at yours? - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:45: And in Tractate Chagigah, concerning what they said in the Mishnah (chapter 2, mishnah 1), "whoever has no regard for the honor of his Maker, it would have been fitting for him not to have come into the world" - they said in the Talmud (16a), what is this? Rabbi Abba said, this is one who gazes at the rainbow; Rav Yosef said, this is one who commits a transgression in secret. One who gazes at the rainbow - as it is written (Ezekiel 1:28), "like the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud on a day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around; it was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:46: And concerning the punishment of one who blemishes his sight, it is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Pekudei (page 263a), in one of the palaces of impurity - they said, of blessed memory: beneath this appointee stands another appointee, over whom are a thousand and ten thousand [subordinates], and this appointee is called "Patut" - this is the one who entices people and leads them astray, to gaze and look at what is unnecessary for them, in many acts of harlotry and adultery. And all those with him all stand by him and walk before him, and force him to lead his eyes astray, to gaze at what is unnecessary - and this is "Sarserim," who is the evil broker for all those evils. This one stands over the grave from the time that body is judged, and breaks his eyes, because he profited from them while he was in this world, and they are his - and in this place the soul is judged, until it enters that place called "Bor" [pit], where there are many snakes and scorpions that all sting that soul and take hold of it and judge it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:47: And the reason that the punishment of one who blemishes his sight is in this first palace and not in the other palaces, it appears to me, is because whoever blemishes his sight blemishes the Shechinah, who is the pupil of the eye from which the light emerges - and therefore, in exchange, corresponding to it, is the cleansing of the soul from the blemish. And everything they said, "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing," that one should not gaze, and so on, is because in gazing at an evil thing, these are the powers of Lilith that spread from this palace - for "evil" [ra] is Samael, and "an evil thing" is Lilith and her powers, which are the causes that bring a person to become "evil" and pour out semen in vain, which is called "evil" - and therefore his own powers, through which he sinned, are the ones that exact punishment, along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Korach, page 177a), "for He shall pay man according to his deed" (Job 34:11).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:48: And because the blemish of sight is so great, as we have elaborated, we find in the Midrash that Rabbi Matya ben Charash drove nails into his eyes so as not to stumble - it says in the Midrash, copied in the Yalkut (Parashat Vayechi, siman 161, page 49, col. 3), on the verse (Genesis 49:22), "Joseph is a fruitful son" - the story of Rabbi Matya ben Charash, who was sitting in the study hall occupied with Torah, and the radiance of his face was like the sun, and his facial features resembled the ministering angels, for he had never in his life raised his eyes to a woman in the world. Once Satan passed by and became jealous of him, and said, is it possible that a man like this has not sinned? He said before the Holy One, blessed be He, Master of the universe, what is Rabbi Matya ben Charash before You? He said to him, he is a completely righteous man. He said before Him, give me permission and I shall entice him. He said to him, you cannot prevail over him. He said, nevertheless. He said to him, go. He appeared to him as the most beautiful woman there had ever been since the days of Na'amah, the sister of Tuval-Kayin, over whom the ministering angels erred, as it is said (Genesis 6:2), "and the sons of God saw the daughters of man." She stood before him. As soon as he saw her, he turned his face away and put it behind him. Again she came and stood at his left side; he turned his face to the right side. She kept turning to face him from every side. He said, I fear lest the evil inclination overpower me and cause me to sin. What did that righteous man do? He called that disciple who served before him and said to him, go and bring me fire and nails. He brought him nails, and he put them into his eyes. When Satan saw this, he shuddered and fell backward. At that moment the Holy One, blessed be He, called Raphael and said to him, go and heal Rabbi Matya ben Charash. He came and stood before him. He said to him, who are you? He said to him, I am Raphael, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, sent to heal your eyes. He said to him, leave me; what has happened has happened. Raphael returned before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said before Him, Master of the universe, so and so did Matya say to me. He said to him, go and tell him, I am guarantor that the evil inclination shall not rule over him. He immediately healed him. From here the Sages said, whoever does not gaze at women, all the more so at his fellow's wife, the evil inclination does not rule over him - to this point, their wording.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:49: And after we have spoken of the blemish of the eyes, let us speak of their repair. It is a commandment to gaze with one's eyes at the creations of the Creator, as David said (Psalms 8:4), "when I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars that You have established; what is man, that You are mindful of him." And likewise to gaze at the commandment of tzitzit, as it is said (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall see it and remember," and so on. And likewise, if he sees a Torah scroll, or a sage, or an elder passing before him, he should rise before him and honor him according to the commandment, and not avert his eyes so as not to see him and [thus avoid having to] rise - for concerning this commandment it is said (Leviticus 19:32), "before the aged you shall rise," and so on, "and you shall fear your God." And in Sefer Chasidim it is written, that if he was standing and saw an elder [approaching from a distance], before he reaches him he should sit down, so that when he comes to pass before him, the rising will be for the sake of the commandment and not merely out of habit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:50: And Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 1, siman 15), that whoever has sinned with his eyes, his repair is to shed tears with his eyes over his sins, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 119:136), "streams of water run down from my eyes, because they have not kept Your Torah" - he did not say "because I have not kept Your Torah," but "because they have not kept" - and the intent is, [my] eyes have not kept Your Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:51: And among the repairs of the eyes is shedding tears over a worthy person, as they said, of blessed memory, in Tractate Shabbat (105a), on the verse (Psalms 56:9), "You count my wanderings; put my tears into Your bottle - are they not in Your record?" - Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the name of Bar Kappara: whoever sheds tears over a worthy person, the Holy One, blessed be He, counts them and places them in His treasury, as it is said, "put my tears into Your bottle - are they not in Your record?" - to this point. And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, end of page 57), in these words: and whoever grieves over the loss of the righteous, or sheds tears over them, the Holy One, blessed be He, proclaims concerning him (Isaiah 6:7), "your iniquity is removed, and your sin atoned for" - and not only that, but his sons shall not die in his lifetime, and concerning him it is written (ibid. 53:10), "he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:52: And Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (cf. gate 4, siman 50), that the repair of the eyes is to rise in the night watch and not sleep the whole night. And it appears to me that David intended this in saying (Psalms 119:148), "my eyes anticipate the night watches, to meditate on Your word" - along the lines of (ibid. 119:136), "streams of water run down from my eyes," which Rabbeinu Yonah explained - the intent being that the eyes that sinned should banish sleep from themselves and anticipate the night watch to occupy themselves with Torah. And I found support for this in the Tikkunim (page 145a), in these words: and the eyes that shine through Torah, of them it is said (Psalms 145:15), "the eyes of all look expectantly to You, and You give them their food in due season" - and a person must occupy himself with them constantly, evening, morning, and noon, [before] the Holy One, blessed be He - this is what is written (Deuteronomy 11:12), "always, the eyes of the LORD your God are upon it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year" - and we learn "always" from "always" - the "always" of evening and morning [i.e., the daily offering] teaches the constant "always, the eyes of the LORD your God are upon it" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:53: And so it appears to me, that the repair of the eyes is when a person gazes with them to read Torah, especially the Written Torah, and especially, of the particular, when he is called up to read from the Torah scroll in the synagogue.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:54: Further, Rabbeinu Tam wrote (Sefer HaYashar, ibid.) that his eyes should be closed during prayer, and that he should place his tefillin between his eyes. However, in saying that his eyes should be closed during prayer, this refers specifically to the Amidah prayer, which is prayed standing, and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Va'etchanan, page 260b), in these words: come and see, whoever stands in prayer must direct his feet [together] - as they established - and must cover his head, as one who sits before the King, and must cover his eyes, so as not to gaze at the Shechinah. And in the writing of Rav Hamnuna Sabba it says: whoever opens his eyes during prayer, or does not lower his eyes to the ground, the Angel of Death advances against him, and when his soul departs, he shall not gaze at the illumination of the Shechinah and shall not die by a kiss. Whoever disdains the Shechinah is himself disdained at the hour he needs Her - this is what is written (1 Samuel 2:30), "for those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed." This one who gazes at the Shechinah at the time he is praying - but how can he gaze at the Shechinah? Rather, he should know for certain that the Shechinah stands before him - this is what is written (Isaiah 38:2), "and Hezekiah turned his face to the wall" - for there the Shechinah rests, and therefore he did not wish anything to intervene between him and the wall - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:55: And the rest of his wording, where he says "and must cover his eyes," it appears that, first and foremost, one should cover his eyes with the tallit of the commandment upon him - since it does not say "he should not open his eyes," as it says afterward, "whoever opens his eyes" or "does not lower his eyes," and further down concerning the punishment - therefore it says that if, at the very least, he does not lower his eyes, even though they remain open, or if he closes and does not open them, even though they are not lowered, he is punished - but the better way is that he cover them, and so I have seen pious sages practice - the pious sage Rabbi Elazar ibn Yochai, peace be upon him, and my teacher, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:56: And during the rest of the order of prayer, it is good that he lower his eyes so as not to look beyond four cubits - for this is something a person is obligated to fulfill always, and at the very least he should not transgress this repair of having humble eyes at the time of prayer - for if he is haughty of eyes, he pushes the Shechinah away from him, as it is written (Psalms 101:5), "haughty of eyes," and so on, "him I cannot endure" - and how can his prayer be properly directed if the Shechinah is not with him?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:57: And my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote concerning (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall not go about after your heart," something relevant to this discourse, and I saw fit to copy the sum of his words here. The summary of his words is that everything that enters through sight is physical, and therefore a person must close his eyes at the time of prayer, for by removing his eyes from the physical he shall think of the spiritual - and this is his saying, "and you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes" - the physical ones - "but rather after My heart and My eyes," which are the supernal sefirot. "After which you go astray [zonim]" - for it is the way of a person, from the side of his soul, to be drawn after the subtle spiritual things, and when he thinks of the physical he is outside his nature, like a harlot [zonah], who is called such because she does what is outside the way of her nature. And therefore a person must purify his thoughts, for just as he would be ashamed to commit a transgression because of shame before the Creator, so he should be ashamed before Him that He see him thinking something contrary to His will, for the thought is revealed before Him like the deed, as it is said (Jeremiah 17:10), "I the LORD search the heart, I test the kidneys" - to this point, the sum of his words on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:58: And with this introduction we shall understand our saying, in the Sabbath prayer liturgy, in "V'Yishtabach" (or similar), "for every eye looks expectantly to You" - and the intent is that the eye was not built to look expectantly at physical things, but rather to be like the eyes of the prophets, who would look expectantly at the supernal chariot in those spiritual visions - and this is attained only through closing the eye and concealing it from physical things, as explained, and also through guarding the eye from things that blemish it. And therefore the early pious ones were called "open-eyed," as found in the Zohar in several supplements (Parashat Yitro, page 74a) - the reason being that they merited proper sight to such a degree that no curtain separated between them and holiness. Among these you find Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, peace be upon him, in the story of that gentile who took a purse, and so on, where it says that he could see with his eye all things, even distant ones (Tosefot, page 4, side b). And similarly, concerning the wisdom of physiognomy, explained in Parashat Yitro (Zohar, Parashat Yitro, from page 70a), that twenty-two letters are imprinted on the forehead, and through them the sages see. And similarly, Rav Hamnuna, who would sit on Sabbath eve to see the delight of souls, these ascending and these descending, in Parashat Terumah (cf. page 136b). And concerning something similar to this they said in Tractate Derech Eretz (chapter 4), in these words: your eyes, which you have not set on money that is not yours, shall shine for you in the darkness of blindness, as it is said (Isaiah 58:10), "and your light shall shine in darkness" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:59: And concerning the virtue of one who guards his sight and does not follow the sight of his eyes, they said in Tractate Kallah (chapter 2), in these words: Rabbi Yochi bar Yoshiyahu said, whoever gazes at women will eventually come to sin, and whoever turns himself away from a transgression and does not commit it, even if he is [merely] an Israelite, deserves to offer a burnt offering like a High Priest upon the altar, as it is said (Exodus 24:5), "and he sent the young men of the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings." And whoever makes himself lazy toward a transgression and does not commit it is nourished by the radiance of the Shechinah like the ministering angels, as it is said (ibid. 24:11), "and they beheld God, and did eat and drink" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 8:60: Further, they said, of blessed memory, in Bava Batra (cf. Vayikra Rabbah 23:13): Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, [said], whoever sees a matter of nakedness and does not feast his eyes upon it merits and receives the countenance of the Shechinah. What is the reason? (Isaiah 33:15), "who shuts his eyes from looking upon evil" - what is written right after it? (ibid. 33:17), "your eyes shall behold the King in His beauty" - to this point, their wording. And the reason for receiving the countenance of the Shechinah through guarding one's sight is simple, in light of what we explained above, that a "matter of nakedness" is the external force - "a matter of nakedness" [davar ervah] indeed, for every "ervah" [nakedness] is "ra" [evil] plus "Vav-Heh," as explained in the Tikkunim (page 99a) - and since he guards himself not to separate the union of Vav-Heh, it is fitting that he receive the countenance of the Shechinah, and the countenance of the Shechinah is the union - to be further explained below, with God's help. And this is his saying (Isaiah 33:17), "the King in His beauty" - rather, the intent is in the secret of union, namely the sixth attribute [Tiferet], in which is the secret of beauty; and likewise the ninth attribute [Yesod], namely (Genesis 39:6), "and Joseph was of beautiful form" - and this is what is explained at the beginning of the chapter, that in blemishing sight one blemishes the pupil, and the light of the pupil - and since he did not blemish them and was saved, he repaired the supernal union, and therefore his soul shall merit to receive the illumination of the supernal union. And with this is included the matter of the repair of the eyes and the virtue of guarding them in their repair.
